approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would update and strengthen the rules governing Australia's intelligence agencies, mainly the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation.

It would put into effect the government's response to a parliamentary committee's 22 recommendations and also adopt seven further measures suggested in a later inquiry, which mostly involve technical changes to improve oversight, clarify legal fault elements, and narrow some exceptions to offences about leaking sensitive information.

The bill would enhance intelligence agency capabilities in seven areas, including updating ASIO's employment rules, overhauling its warrant-based collection powers, boosting its ability to run covert operations with safeguards, improving information sharing, protecting intelligence-related information and the identities of personnel, and renaming some Defence agencies.
The bill would modernise ASIO's employment framework.
It would streamline ASIO's warrant-based intelligence collection powers.
It would strengthen ASIO's capacity for covert operations, with oversight.
It would clarify and improve rules for ASIO's cooperation and information sharing.
It would enhance capabilities of agencies covered by the IS Act.
It would improve protection of intelligence information and personnel identities, and rename some Defence agencies.
The Australian Intelligence Community, particularly ASIO, and Defence agencies.

Introduced the National Security Legislation Amendment Bill (No 1) 2014, implementing 22 recommendations from a 2012-13 parliamentary inquiry, which modernises ASIO's employment and warrant powers unchanged for about 30 years and raises the maximum penalty for unauthorised disclosure of intelligence information from two to 10 years imprisonment.

Argued that Labor will support the National Security Legislation Amendment Bill as amended, tracing its origins to a 2012 inquiry that received 240 submissions and 29 exhibits from more than 130 stakeholders, and welcomed Senate amendments requiring special intelligence operations to be approved by the Attorney-General and exempting disclosures to a person's lawyer or the Inspector-General from the new secrecy offence.

Opposed elements of the National Security Legislation Amendment Bill, warning it could jail journalists and whistleblowers for reporting matters like the past bugging of East Timorese offices, and moved a Greens amendment to cap the number of devices accessible under a single computer access warrant at 20.

Criticised the government and opposition for rushing the National Security Legislation Amendment Bill through with barely any speakers, noting the 2013 parliamentary committee had recommended an exposure draft for public consultation that was never released, and questioned why the penalty for media disclosure of a special intelligence operation was being raised from two years to 10.

Announced she would not support the National Security Legislation Amendment Bill, citing the Law Council of Australia's concerns about the tight inquiry timeframe limiting scrutiny, and describing fear among her Indi constituents who told her they were avoiding overseas weddings and city football matches out of terrorism anxiety.

Opposed elements of the National Security Legislation Amendment Bill, quoting a 2004 UK House of Lords dissent warning that laws restricting freedom pose a greater threat to national life than terrorism itself, and noted a recent counter-terrorism raid deployed 800 police officers for a single arrest just as parliament debated the new anti-terror powers.

Argued that the offence concerning reckless disclosure of special intelligence operations is necessary because disclosure can endanger participants and their families, while noting the prosecution must prove knowledge of a substantial risk and unjustifiable conduct.

Argued that the government opposes the member for Denison's amendments extending the intelligence committee's oversight to operational activities, saying that role is already comprehensively covered by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security under its 1986 act, and moved that the question be put.
